questions.prompt: Which description matches the book’s definition of a database?
choices: A list of files that can only be read by one program
A set of commands that changes stored records
A collection of related data with implicit meaning
A collection of facts chosen without regard to their meaning
questions.explanation: A database is a collection of related data, and data consists of known facts that can be recorded and have implicit meaning (§1.1).

questions.prompt: Which collection is designed as a database rather than an arbitrary pile of facts?
choices: A temporary list of unrelated values copied from several public pages
A folder of measurements with no defined relationships or intended users
A set of program instructions that describe how to print a report
An organization’s student records, built to support registration and grading
questions.explanation: A database represents a miniworld as a logically coherent collection and is built for a specific purpose and intended users (§1.1).

questions.prompt: In the UNIVERSITY example, what does a coding scheme do for the STUDENT class value?
choices: It uses agreed values such as 1 through 5 to represent class categories
It checks whether a student has completed course prerequisites
It assigns each student a different course number
It stores the student’s grades in a separate file
questions.explanation: The example codes freshman through graduate student as values 1 through 5, respectively (§1.2).

questions.prompt: For the UNIVERSITY database, which actions change stored data rather than retrieve it? Select all that apply.
choices: List the prerequisites of the Database course
Add a new section for the Database course
List the names and grades of students in a specified section
Change Smith’s class from freshman to sophomore
questions.explanation: Adding a section and changing Smith’s class are updates. Listing grades or prerequisites retrieves information (§1.2).

questions.prompt: What is metadata in the self-describing database approach?
choices: The current student, course, and grade records themselves
The application programs that send requests to the DBMS
The results returned by the most recent query
The catalog’s description of database structure and constraints
questions.explanation: Metadata is descriptive information stored in the catalog, including the structure and constraints of the database (§1.3.1).

questions.prompt: Which traits distinguish the database approach from traditional file processing? Select all that apply.
choices: Each application embeds its own fixed file definitions
A catalog describes the database structure and constraints
Different users can work with views of shared data
Concurrent transactions are managed so updates remain controlled
questions.explanation: The database approach includes a catalog, support for multiple views, and shared data with multiuser transaction processing. Embedding file definitions in each application is characteristic of traditional file processing (§1.3).

questions.prompt: A STUDENT record gains a birth-date field. Why can a DBMS access program often keep working without a code change?
choices: A view prevents the database schema from changing
The new field is stored only in the application’s query results
The DBMS stores the file structure in its catalog separately from access programs
The DBMS automatically converts every old file into a new application
questions.explanation: Because the catalog describes the data structure separately from access programs, changing the catalog’s STUDENT description can preserve program-data independence (§1.3.2).

questions.prompt: A university keeps student, course, and grade data in one database. How can the transcript office and prerequisite reviewers each see a useful presentation of that data?
choices: Let each group define a view containing the data it needs
Move the grade records into the catalog
Require both groups to use the same query results
Give each group a separate copy of every database file
questions.explanation: A view can be a subset of stored data or include derived data, allowing each user group to work with a relevant perspective on the database (§1.3.3).

questions.prompt: Two reservation transactions try to assign the same seat. Which statement correctly describes isolation and atomicity?
choices: Isolation chooses the fastest query plan; atomicity prevents users from reading the database
Isolation permits only one transaction per database; atomicity saves a copy before every query
Isolation makes each transaction appear independent; atomicity makes all its operations happen or none happen
Isolation makes all operations permanent; atomicity allows transactions to see one another’s partial work
questions.explanation: Isolation makes a transaction appear to execute independently of concurrent transactions; atomicity ensures that all operations in the transaction execute or none do (§1.3.4).

questions.prompt: Which responsibilities belong to a database administrator (DBA)? Select all that apply.
choices: Coordinate and monitor database use
Choose record structures by gathering prospective users’ requirements
Acquire needed hardware and software resources
Authorize access to the database
questions.explanation: The DBA authorizes access, coordinates and monitors use, and acquires resources as needed. Identifying data and choosing structures are database-design responsibilities (§1.4.1–1.4.2).

questions.prompt: Which descriptions correctly match database end-user categories? Select all that apply.
choices: Casual users make occasional, varied requests; standalone users maintain personal databases with ready-made packages
Parametric users repeatedly perform standard database tasks through carefully programmed canned transactions
Sophisticated users learn DBMS facilities and build applications for complex requirements
System analysts maintain personal databases with ready-made packages; DBAs run canned transactions as their main task
questions.explanation: Casual, parametric, sophisticated, and standalone users are described across the first three choices: standalone users maintain personal databases with packaged software. The final choice confuses those end-user categories with analyst and DBA responsibilities (§1.4.1, §1.4.3–1.4.4).

questions.prompt: One team gathers end-user needs and specifies routine transactions; another codes and maintains them. Which roles are being performed, in that order?
choices: Application programmer, then system analyst
System analyst, then application programmer
Database designer, then operator
DBA, then database designer
questions.explanation: System analysts determine requirements and specify canned transactions; application programmers implement, test, and maintain them (§1.4.4).

questions.prompt: Which jobs are workers behind the scene in a database environment? Select all that apply.
choices: Tool developers who create optional database tools
Operators and maintenance personnel who run the system environment
Casual users who formulate occasional interactive queries
DBMS system designers and implementers
questions.explanation: DBMS implementers, tool developers, and operations or maintenance personnel are workers behind the scene. Casual users are actors on the scene (§1.5).

questions.prompt: A person maintains the database server’s hardware and software environment but does not use the database contents for a daily task. Which category fits?
choices: Database designer
Operator and maintenance personnel
Sophisticated end user
System analyst
questions.explanation: Operators and maintenance personnel are responsible for running and maintaining the hardware and software environment (§1.5).

questions.prompt: A database stores a repeated student name to speed up a grade lookup. What should the DBMS do to reduce the risk of conflicting copies?
choices: Treat each copy as unrelated data and allow it to change independently
Remove the catalog entry for the original student record
Control the intentional redundancy with consistency checks
Prevent users from retrieving the grade report
questions.explanation: Controlled redundancy can improve query performance, but the DBMS should check that duplicated values agree with their corresponding records (§1.6.1).

questions.prompt: An employee may view salary data but is not allowed to change it. How can a DBMS enforce that restriction?
choices: Use account authorization that distinguishes retrieval from update privileges
Store the salary in a view that every user can modify
Turn off integrity constraints for the employee’s account
Give the employee a separate copy of the database
questions.explanation: A DBMS authorization subsystem can restrict users by account and control retrieval and update operations separately (§1.6.2).

questions.prompt: When is a program object called persistent?
choices: When it is defined in a database catalog but never stored
When it can be used only while the creating program is running
When it survives program termination and can later be retrieved
When it is copied into a query plan before each update
questions.explanation: A persistent object survives the end of program execution and can later be retrieved (§1.6.3).

questions.prompt: Which DBMS mechanisms can help execute disk-based queries efficiently? Select all that apply.
choices: Buffers that keep some database pages in main memory
A query optimizer that chooses an execution plan
A backup copy that replaces query processing
Indexes that provide search paths to records
questions.explanation: Indexes speed searches, buffering keeps database parts in memory, and query optimization chooses an efficient execution plan. Backup supports recovery rather than query execution (§1.6.4–1.6.5).

questions.prompt: Which data-entry problems can the DBMS reject automatically when the corresponding constraints are defined? Select all that apply.
choices: A grade uses a value outside its permitted data type
Two course records use the same value for a unique course number
A grade is validly recorded as C even though the student earned A
A section refers to a course record that does not exist
questions.explanation: Defined type, uniqueness, and referential-integrity constraints can reject invalid values, duplicate keys, and broken references. A valid grade entered incorrectly may satisfy the defined constraints and go undetected (§1.6.8).

questions.prompt: Which additional capabilities or organizational effects does the section identify for the database approach? Select all that apply.
choices: Once running, a database prevents later changes to application requirements
Triggers can invoke additional operations in response to updates to a table
The DBA can set shared naming and formatting standards across departments and users
A database can reduce development time for new reports and adapt as requirements evolve
questions.explanation: The section describes triggers, organization-wide standards, reduced time for new application development, and flexibility as requirements change. The last choice contradicts that flexibility (§1.6.9–1.6.10).

questions.prompt: Why were early hierarchical and network database systems harder to adapt to new queries?
choices: They stored every data item in a catalog instead of a database
They required all user groups to work from separate databases
They relied on high-level query languages that hid all relationships
Their storage organization was closely tied to conceptual relationships and programs
questions.explanation: Early systems tied data storage organization closely to their conceptual structures and programs, making new access patterns and reorganizations difficult (§1.7.1).

questions.prompt: Why did relational systems make new queries and changing requirements easier to handle than earlier systems?
choices: They replaced database schemas with unstructured files
They separated physical storage from conceptual representation and offered high-level query languages
They required application programmers to rewrite the storage system for each request
They linked each query to a fixed physical record path
questions.explanation: Relational systems separated physical storage from conceptual representation and introduced high-level query languages, improving query flexibility and adaptation (§1.7.2).

questions.prompt: A service stores posts at very large scale and needs fast retrieval of nontraditional data. Which database trend in the chapter addresses this kind of need?
choices: Hierarchical systems that require a new program for each query
Object databases used exclusively for small personal databases
Big-data and NOSQL systems, with storage choices suited to application requirements
Traditional file systems that store only fixed-length numeric records
questions.explanation: The chapter describes big-data and NOSQL systems as emerging to manage massive data stores, including nontraditional data, with choices shaped by application requirements (§1.7.6).

questions.prompt: Which costs can contribute to the overhead of using a general-purpose DBMS? Select all that apply.
choices: Initial hardware, software, and training investment
Generality in defining and processing data
Security, concurrency, recovery, and integrity functions
A guarantee that every application meets strict real-time deadlines
questions.explanation: The book lists initial investment and training, DBMS generality, and overhead from security, concurrency, recovery, and integrity functions. A DBMS does not guarantee strict timing (§1.8).

questions.prompt: A fixed, single-user embedded application has very limited storage and strict timing requirements. Why might a general-purpose DBMS be a poor fit?
choices: It cannot support a customized application program
It cannot store data for an application with fixed requirements
Its generality and resource demands may outweigh its benefits under these constraints
It requires every user to make occasional interactive queries
questions.explanation: The book identifies fixed applications, stringent real-time needs, limited embedded storage, and lack of multiple users as cases where a general-purpose DBMS’s overhead may not be worthwhile (§1.8).
